endorsements.quote: Evaluation strategies must therefore distinguish performance in silent settings from effectiveness in implemented workflows, where confounding and feedback loops may affect observed performance if the causal relationships among AI outputs, interventions, and outcomes are not considered [ 12 ].

Determining whether an AI‐enabled workflow is effective requires causal evaluation, ideally through randomization when feasible and, in routine deployment, often through quasi‐experimental causal inference designs.
Silent deployment allows assessment of local validity and subgroup performance before model outputs are incorporated into a clinical workflow.

Assessing whether the system appropriately identifies cases requiring human escalation is particularly important for determining whether the current oversight configuration is safe and whether escalation criteria require refinement.
Once AI‐drafted content is shown to humans for review, RWE can be generated directly from observable review behavior.

unlisted_practices: Adjudicate discrepancies between AI outputs and human reviewers to distinguish AI error from human error when using human review as a reference standard.
Establish escalation criteria before automated implementation, potentially through prior human-on-the-loop evaluation.
Quantify residual human follow-up work in automated deployments once escalation pathways have demonstrated sufficient reliability.
Use causal inference methods, such as quasi-experimental designs, to distinguish intervention effects from algorithmic drift when evaluating deployed predictive AI.
Complement real-world evidence with qualitative or mixed-methods data collection to clarify adoption, user reliance, and workarounds.
Align local quality-improvement measures with the intervention's goals, including outcome, process, and balancing measures.

screen.reason: This is a framework/commentary paper proposing approaches and study designs to generate real-world evidence (RWE) across different deployment configurations (silent, HITL, HOTL, automated) for health systems.
